Meccan, according to all of them.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿By the sun and its brightness﴾. These are two oaths: an oath by the sun, and an oath by its brightness (*ḍuḥāhā*). Regarding *ḍuḥāhā* there are four interpretations:

The first is its shining, as said by Mujāhid.

The second is its spreading out, as said by al-Yazīdī.

The third is its heat, as said by al-Suddī.

The fourth is this daytime, as said by Qatādah.

It may also admit a fifth meaning: that it is what appears by it from every created being, so the oath is by it and by all created things.

﴿And by the moon when it follows it﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations:

The first: when it matches it (*idhā sāwāhā*), as said by Mujāhid.

The second: when it follows it, as said by Ibn ʿAbbās.

Regarding its following of the sun there are three interpretations:

The first: the first night of the month, when the sun sets and the moon is seen at its setting, as said by Qatādah.

The second: the fifteenth of the month, when the moon rises at the sunset, as said by al-Ṭabarī.

The third: throughout the whole month. In the first half it follows the sun, being ahead of it while the sun is behind it; and when it is in the last half, it is ahead of the sun while the sun is behind it, as said by Ibn Zayd.

It may admit a fourth meaning: that it follows the sun at night, so the moon has a share of the night just as the sun has a share of the day, since the influence of each of them is in its own time. The sun has the day, and the moon has the night.

﴿And by the day when it displays it﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations:

The first: it illuminated it, meaning the sun, because its light by day reveals (*yujallī*) the darkness of the night, as said by Mujāhid.

The second: it made it manifest, because the sun's appearance is by day. From this is the saying of Qays ibn al-Khaṭīm:

*"She is brought to us like the sun between clouds; an edge of her appeared, and she withheld her edge."*

It may admit a third meaning: that the day revealed what is in the earth of its living beings, which were hidden by night and became visible by day spreading out.

﴿And by the night when it covers it﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations:

The first: it darkened it, meaning the sun, and this is what Mujāhid's view implies.

The second: it conceals it. From this is the saying of al-Khansāʾ:

*"I pasture the stars, though I was not charged with their pasturing, and at times I cover myself with the excess of my rags."*

﴿And by the heaven and He who built it﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations:

The first: "and the heaven and its building," as said by Qatādah.

The second: its meaning is "and He who built it," who is God, exalted is He, as said by Mujāhid and al-Ḥasan.

It may admit a third meaning: "and the heaven and what is in its building," meaning the angels and the stars. In that case this is an oath by what is in the heaven, and what preceded it is an oath by what is on the earth.

﴿And by the earth and He who spread it out﴾. Regarding this there are three interpretations:

The first: its meaning is that He spread it out, as said by Sufyān and Abū Ṣāliḥ.

The second: its meaning is that He divided it, as said by Ibn ʿAbbās.

The third: it means what He created in it, as said by ʿAṭiyya al-ʿAwfī, and *ṭaḥāhā* carries the meaning of "created it." The poet said:

*"Jadhīmah does not know who made it, nor who dwells in the lofty Throne."*

It may admit a fourth meaning: that it is what came out of it of plants, springs and treasures, because that is life for what was created upon it.

﴿And a soul and He who proportioned it﴾. Regarding "soul" there are two views:

The first: it is Ādam, and "He who proportioned it" is God, exalted is He, as said by al-Ḥasan.

The second: it is every soul.

Regarding the meaning of "proportioned it" according to this view, there are two interpretations:

The first: He made them equal in health, and He made them equal in punishment altogether, as said by Ibn Jurayj.

The second: He proportioned its form and balanced its creation, as said by Mujāhid.

It may admit a third meaning: He proportioned it through the intellect by which He favored it over all the animals.

﴿Then He inspired it with its wickedness and its righteousness﴾. Regarding "inspired" (*alhamahā*) there are two interpretations:

The first: He made it aware of them (*aʿlamahā*), as said by Mujāhid.

The second: He obliged it to them (*alzamahā*), as said by Ibn Jubayr.

Regarding "its wickedness and its righteousness" there are three interpretations:

The first: misery and happiness, as said by Mujāhid.

The second: evil and good, as said by Ibn ʿAbbās.

The third: obedience and disobedience, as said by al-Ḍaḥḥāk.

It may admit a fourth meaning: fear and desire, because they are the two callers to wickedness and righteousness.

Juwaybir narrated from al-Ḍaḥḥāk, from Ibn ʿAbbās, that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to, when he recited this verse, ﴿Then He inspired it with its wickedness and its righteousness﴾, raise his voice: "O God, grant my soul its righteousness; You are its Guardian and its Master, and You are the best of those who purify it."

﴿He has succeeded who purifies it﴾. Upon this the oath was sworn. Ibn ʿAbbās said: "In it there are eleven oaths."

Regarding this there are two interpretations:

The first: he has succeeded who has had God purify his soul through obedience to God and righteous deeds.

The second: he has succeeded who has purified his own soul through obedience to God and righteous deeds.

Regarding "purifies it" (*zakkāhā*) there are two interpretations:

The first: he cleansed it, which is the view of Mujāhid.

The second: he set it right, which is the view of Saʿīd ibn Jubayr.

﴿And he has failed who corrupts it﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations:

The first: according to what He decreed, "and he has failed who has had God corrupt his soul."

The second: "he who corrupts his own soul."

Regarding "corrupts it" (*dassāhā*) there are seven interpretations:

The first: he led it astray and misguided it, as said by Mujāhid and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, because he corrupted his own soul with acts of disobedience. From this is the saying of the poet:

*"It was you who buried ʿAmr, so that their widows among them became destitute and forsaken orphans."*

The second: its sin and its wickedness, as said by Qatādah.

The third: its loss, as said by ʿIkrimah.

The fourth: its lying, as said by Ibn ʿAbbās.

The fifth: he made it wretched, as said by Ibn Salām.

The sixth: he kept it away from good, and this is the view of al-Ḍaḥḥāk.

The seventh: he hid it and kept it obscure through stinginess, related by Ibn ʿĪsā.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 91, verse 11–15:

﴿Thamud denied [their prophet] in their rebellion﴾. Concerning this there are three interpretations:
One: "in their rebellion" means in their transgression and disobedience. This is the view of Mujahid and Qatadah.

The second: "in all of them" (i.e., in all of their [deeds]). This is the view of Muhammad ibn Ka'b.

The third: "in their punishment." This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

They said: the name of the punishment that came upon them was al-Tagwa (the rebellion).

﴿So their Lord brought down destruction upon them for their sin, and leveled it [over them]﴾. Concerning this there are three meanings:

One: its meaning is "so He became angry with them."

The second: its meaning is "so He closed over them."

The third: its meaning is "so He destroyed them completely," and it is similar to damdama; it is a word in Abyssinian (Ethiopic) that the Arabs spoke.

﴿And He made them equal﴾. Concerning this there are two meanings:

One: "He made them equal among themselves in destruction." This is the view of al-Suddi and Yahya ibn Salam.

The second: "He leveled the earth over them." This is mentioned by Ibn Shajarah.

It may also bear a third meaning: "He made equal those who came after them of the nations."

﴿And He does not fear its consequence﴾. Concerning this there are two meanings:

One: "And Allah does not fear the consequence of what He did to them of destruction." This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: "He who hamstrung her does not fear the consequence of what he did of hamstringing her." This is the view of al-Hasan.

It may also bear a third meaning: "And Salih does not fear the consequence of hamstringing her, because he had warned them, and Allah the Exalted saved him when He destroyed them."
